quizzes.title: Quick-Fire Sums
quizzes.description: Warm up the room with fast mental arithmetic everyone can have a go at.

questions.q: What is 7 × 8?
questions.note: A handy memory trick: 5, 6, 7, 8 — 56 = 7 × 8.

questions.q: What is 18 + 27?
questions.note: Accept 'forty-five'; 18 + 20 = 38, then add 7.

questions.q: What is 144 ÷ 12?
questions.note: 144 is also called a 'gross', meaning twelve dozen.

questions.q: Half of 250 is 125.
questions.note: 125 is also 5 × 5 × 5.

questions.q: What is 25% of 80?
questions.note: 25% is a quarter, so just divide 80 by 4.

questions.q: How many minutes are there in three and a half hours?
questions.note: 3 hours is 180 minutes, plus 30 more makes 210.

questions.q: What is 11 × 11?
questions.note: Accept 'one hundred and twenty-one'; 11 × 11 × 11 = 1,331.

questions.q: What is 0.5 + 0.25?
questions.note: A half plus a quarter makes three quarters.

quizzes.title: Shape Up
quizzes.description: Sides, angles, faces and circles — a tour of everyday geometry.

questions.q: How many sides does a nonagon have?
questions.note: 'Nona' comes from the Latin word for ninth.

questions.q: How many edges does a cube have?
questions.note: A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 corners (vertices).

questions.q: A square is a special type of rectangle.
questions.note: A square is a rectangle whose four sides are all equal.

questions.q: What is the area, in square centimetres, of a rectangle 8 cm long and 5 cm wide?
questions.note: Accept '40 cm²'; area of a rectangle is length × width.

questions.q: What is the name for a triangle whose three sides are all different lengths?
questions.note: An isosceles triangle has at least two equal sides.

questions.q: What do the interior angles of any quadrilateral add up to?
questions.note: Any quadrilateral splits into two triangles, and 2 × 180° = 360°.

questions.q: A circle has exactly two lines of symmetry.
questions.note: A circle has infinitely many lines of symmetry — every diameter is one.

questions.q: What is a straight line from the centre of a circle to its edge called?
questions.note: The diameter is twice the length of the radius.

questions.q: How many faces does a triangular prism have?
questions.note: Accept 'five'; two triangular ends and three rectangular sides.

questions.q: A right-angled triangle has shorter sides of 3 and 4. How long is the longest side?
questions.note: By Pythagoras: 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25, and √25 = 5.

quizzes.title: Minds Behind Maths
quizzes.description: The great thinkers, from ancient Greece and India to the modern day, who shaped mathematics.

questions.q: Which Indian mathematician is famously linked with the 'taxicab number' 1729?
questions.note: 1729 is the smallest number that is the sum of two cubes in two different ways.

questions.q: Euclid is often called the 'Father of Geometry'.
questions.note: His book Elements was used to teach geometry for more than 2,000 years.

questions.q: Which Greek thinker is said to have shouted 'Eureka!' in his bath?
questions.note: The story comes from the Roman writer Vitruvius, writing centuries later.

questions.q: India's first satellite, launched in 1975, was named after which ancient mathematician?
questions.note: Aryabhata lived in the 5th and 6th centuries CE.

questions.q: Who developed calculus independently of Isaac Newton?
questions.note: Much of today's calculus notation, such as dx and the ∫ sign, comes from Leibniz.

questions.q: Who was the first woman to win the Fields Medal?
questions.note: The Iranian mathematician Maryam Mirzakhani won it in 2014.

questions.q: Ada Lovelace wrote famous notes about a machine designed by whom?
questions.note: Her notes on the Analytical Engine are often called the first computer program.

questions.q: The Fields Medal in mathematics is awarded every year.
questions.note: It is awarded every four years, to mathematicians under 40.

questions.q: The number e, about 2.718, is named after which Swiss mathematician?
questions.note: Accept 'Leonhard Euler'; e is often called Euler's number.

questions.q: Which mathematician gave his name to the number triangle where each entry is the sum of the two above?
questions.note: The triangle was studied centuries earlier in India, Persia and China.

quizzes.title: Patterns & Puzzles
quizzes.description: Crack the sequences, spot the primes and outsmart the classic brain-teasers.

questions.q: What comes next: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, …?
questions.note: In the Fibonacci sequence each number is the sum of the two before: 8 + 13 = 21.

questions.q: What is the next prime number after 89?
questions.note: 91 = 7 × 13 and 93 = 3 × 31, so neither is prime.

questions.q: The number 1 is a prime number.
questions.note: A prime has exactly two distinct factors, 1 and itself, so 1 does not count.

questions.q: What comes next: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, …?
questions.note: Each term is n × (n + 1), so the next is 6 × 7; the gaps grow by 2 each time.

questions.q: A bat and a ball cost 110 coins in total. The bat costs 100 coins more than the ball. What does the ball cost?
questions.note: Many say 10, but then the bat would cost 110 and the total would be 120.

questions.q: How many prime numbers are there between 1 and 20?
What comes next: 1, 8, 27, 64, …?
questions.note: These are cube numbers: 5 × 5 × 5 = 125.

questions.q: What is the smallest positive whole number divisible by 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6?
questions.note: Accept 'sixty'; it is the lowest common multiple of those numbers.

questions.q: Adding up all the whole numbers from 1 to 10 gives 55.
questions.note: Quick method: 10 × 11 ÷ 2 = 55.

questions.q: Counting squares of every size, how many squares are there on an 8 × 8 chessboard?
questions.note: Add the square numbers 1 + 4 + 9 + … + 64 to get 204.
